case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
key_cases.holding: In an Oregon case, the court held that the in-school seizure and interview of a child by a caseworker and deputy without a warrant, court order, exigency or parental consent violated the Fourth Amendment (though those defendants had qualified immunity), and that the subsequent removal and medical examination also violated the family's rights.
key_cases.relevance: This is the Oregon-origin decision on caseworker and law-enforcement interviews of a child at school; note that the Supreme Court later vacated the Fourth Amendment portion as moot, so it is persuasive rather than binding on that point.
key_cases.quote: we hold that the investigation conducted by Camreta and Alford and the removal and examination instigated by Camreta all violated Sarah and the girls' constitutional rights

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held that it generally may review a constitutional ruling at the behest of a government official who prevailed below on qualified immunity, but that this Oregon case had become moot because the child had grown up and moved away, and it therefore vacated the part of the Ninth Circuit's opinion deciding the Fourth Amendment question about the in-school interview.
key_cases.relevance: This is the disposition that stripped Greene v. Camreta of precedential force on caseworker and deputy interviews of a child at school; the vacated Fourth Amendment holding must never be cited without it.
key_cases.quote: we vacate the part of the Ninth Circuit's opinion that decided the Fourth Amendment issue.

key_cases.holding: The court held Oregon's mandatory abuse-reporting statutes abrogate the psychotherapist-patient privilege only far enough to permit the required report, not to permit the reporter to testify about the privileged communication in a later judicial proceeding.
key_cases.relevance: Applies the same limited-abrogation principle to any privileged professional who is a mandated reporter.
key_cases.quote: the elder abuse reporting statutes only abrogate privileged communications to the extent that a report be submitted

reporting_details: Oregon is not a universal-reporting state: only the “public or private officials” listed in Or. Rev. Stat. § 419B.005(6) must immediately report suspected child abuse, and they report through the centralized Oregon Child Abuse Hotline or to a local law enforcement agency (Or. Rev. Stat. §§ 419B.010(1), 419B.015(1)(a)); the duty is personal to the official regardless of any employer’s internal reporting policy (§ 419B.010(3), (4)), privileged communications to a psychiatrist, psychologist, member of the clergy, attorney or guardian ad litem are excepted (§ 419B.010(1)), failure to report is a Class A violation (§ 419B.010(5)), and any other person may report voluntarily (§ 419B.015(1)(a)).
